structure.heading: PART I
structure.start_phrase: Verizon Communications Inc. (Verizon or the Company) is a holding company that, acting through its subsidiaries, is one of the world’s leading providers of communications, technology, information and entertainment products and services to consumers, businesses and government entities.
structure.summary:
- Company overview: Verizon Communications Inc. is a global holding company providing communications, technology, information, and entertainment products and services, emphasizing mobility, reliable connectivity, security, and control; headquarters in New York City.
- Reportable segments: Two strategic business units—Verizon Consumer Group (Consumer) and Verizon Business Group (Business).
- Portfolio changes: Sale of Verizon Media to an Apollo affiliate completed on September 1, 2021; acquisition of TracFone Wireless, Inc. completed on November 23, 2021.
- Consumer segment:
  - Offerings: Wireless services (including fixed wireless access) and wireline services via Fios fiber network and copper where Fios isn’t available.
  - Footprint: Wireline in nine Mid-Atlantic/Northeastern states and Washington, D.C.; broad U.S. wireless network; wholesale arrangements.
  - 2021 scale and performance: $95.3B revenue (~71% of consolidated); ~115M wireless retail connections; ~7M wireline broadband connections (Fios + DSL); ~4M Fios video connections.
- Business segment:
  - Offerings: Wireless and wireline services including data, video, conferencing, corporate networking, security, managed network services, voice, IoT, and fixed wireless access.
  - Customers and reach: Businesses, government, carriers across the U.S., with select global offerings.
  - 2021 scale and performance: $31.0B revenue (~23% of consolidated); ~27M wireless retail postpaid connections; ~477K wireline broadband connections (Fios + DSL).
- Service and product organization:
  - Consumer: Products/services available to retail customers and resellers (wholesale network access).
  - Business: Organized by customer groups—Small and Medium Business, Global Enterprise, Public Sector and Other, and Wholesale.
- Wireless services: Offered to both Consumer and Business customers on postpaid and prepaid bases, across a broad range of devices.
- Cross-references: Further details noted in MD&A (Overview and Segment Results) and Note 13 to the consolidated financial statements.

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: Item 1. Business
structure.start_phrase:
Verizon Communications Inc. (Verizon or the Company) is a holding company that, acting through its subsidiaries, is one of the world’s 
leading providers of communications, technology, information and entertainment products and services to consumers, businesses and 
government entities.
structure.summary:
- Company overview: Verizon Communications Inc. is a global provider of communications, technology, information and entertainment services, operating through two reportable segments—Verizon Consumer Group and Verizon Business Group. Principal office: New York, NY.

- Portfolio changes: Sold Verizon Media to an Apollo affiliate (Sept 1, 2021); acquired TracFone Wireless, Inc. (Nov 23, 2021).

- Segment highlights (2021):
  - Consumer: $95.3B revenue (~71% of consolidated); ~115M wireless retail connections; ~7M wireline broadband connections (Fios + DSL); ~4M Fios video connections. Offers wireless services/equipment, FWA (5G Home, LTE Home), Fios internet/video/voice, wholesale MVNO access (including TracFone pre-acquisition).
  - Business: $31.0B revenue (~23%); ~27M wireless retail postpaid connections; ~477k wireline broadband connections. Provides wireless and wireline services, networking, security, managed services, voice, conferencing, IoT and FWA.

- Business sub-segments (2021 revenues and focus):
  - Small and Medium Business: $11.8B (~38% of Business); wireless, voice, networking, Fios, security/managed IT.
  - Global Enterprise: $10.2B (~33%); network services, advanced communications, security, core voice/data, IoT connectivity and platforms.
  - Public Sector and Other: $6.3B (~20%); solutions for federal/state/local governments and education, plus fleet/asset management.
  - Wholesale: $2.7B (~9%); data, voice (including TDM/VoIP), local services for carriers.

- Services and plans: Postpaid and prepaid (24M prepaid connections, including ~20M from TracFone acquisition); diverse plan features (unlimited/metered voice/data/text, hotspot, premium content); device payment plans; subsidized plans no longer offered to Consumer but continue for Business.

- Distribution: Combination of direct (company stores, sales/service centers, digital/omnichannel, direct sales), indirect (agents, national retailers, convenience stores), and business-focused channels (resellers, distributors, system integrators).

- Competitive landscape and trends:
  - Intense competition from national carriers (AT&T, T-Mobile), regionals, MVNOs (including cable operators), OTT providers, big tech platforms, and emerging LEO satellite ISPs; potential new entrant pressure from DISH 5G buildout.
  - Key differentiators: network reliability/speed/coverage; pricing and promotions (including device financing and aggressive device offers); customer service; product innovation and convergence; sales/distribution reach.
  - Wireline competition from cable, wireless broadband, VoIP/OTT; continued shift from linear video to OTT and from landline to wireless.

- Networks and technology:
  - Intelligent Edge Network transformation for efficiency, virtualization, automation and edge compute.
  - 5G: Ultra Wideband in parts of 87 cities; 5G Home in parts of 65 cities as of Dec 31, 2021; C-Band deployed in Jan 2022 reaching ~100M POPs by Feb 2022; DSS enables 5G Nationwide alongside 4G.
  - 4G LTE: Covers ~328M people (including LTE in Rural America partners); LTE Home Internet available.
  - Network reliability: densification (small cells, in-building systems, DAS), spectrum additions, redundancy (battery backup, generators, MPLS backbone), and extensive domestic/international roaming.
  - Fios/PON: Fiber-based broadband positioned for rising bandwidth demand; PON increasingly used for business Ethernet access.
  - Global IP network: One of the largest global fiber networks, serving >180 countries; continued packet optical deployment.

- Spectrum position:
  - Low/mid-band: 800 MHz (cellular), PCS, 700 MHz C block, AWS-1/3, 3.5 GHz CBRS, 5 GHz LAA; reallocating 3G spectrum to LTE; DSS for 5G.
  - Millimeter wave: 28 GHz and 37/39 GHz for capacity in high-demand areas.
  - C-Band: Acquired average 161 MHz (3700–3980 MHz) in 2021; began 5G service Jan 2022.
  - Ongoing spectrum swaps/purchases to optimize contiguity and capacity; subject to FCC approvals.

- Human capital:
  - ~118,400 employees as of Dec 31, 2021 (incl. ~800 TracFone), ~89% U.S.-based; emphasis on talent attraction, development, inclusion, and continuous learning.
  - Diversity snapshot: 66.9% male/33.1% female globally; U.S. workforce 53.9% White, 20.1% Black, 11.9% Hispanic, 8.0% Asian, others; U.S. senior leadership: 38.7% women, 34.9% people of color.
  - Labor relations: ~24% union-represented (CWA, IBEW); current CBAs in Mid-Atlantic/Northeast through Aug 5, 2023; engagement with works councils outside U.S.

- Intellectual property: Portfolio of patents, copyrights, trademarks and domain names; active licensing program; periodic third-party IP claims and licensing offers; management does not expect IP expirations to be materially impactful but recognizes potential litigation/royalty risks.

- Regulatory environment:
  - FCC is primary federal regulator; state/local oversight for certain services.
  - Wireless: Spectrum licensing, renewals, open access rules on some bands, E911, roaming, tower siting/zoning; state “terms and conditions” and taxes.
  - Broadband: Currently treated as “information services” with light regulation; potential for reclassification; state net neutrality efforts (e.g., CA, VT) under litigation; Verizon’s open internet commitment.
  - Wireline voice: Legacy telephony as common carrier with heightened regulation; VoIP subject to specific mandates (911, law enforcement).
  - Video: Fios TV regulated similarly to cable; requires local/state franchises with ongoing obligations.
  - Privacy/data security: Compliance with FCC/FTC oversight, GDPR, CCPA and expanding state/international laws; rising regulatory scrutiny.
  - Public safety/cybersecurity: Emergency communications/alerting requirements; potential cybersecurity regulation; restrictions on certain vendors; disaster continuity rules (e.g., CA backup power).
  - Intercarrier compensation and business data services: FCC oversight of certain rates/terms; Verizon both buys and sells these services.
  - COVID-19: Evolving policies and consumer protection measures introduce operational uncertainty.

- Investor information: SEC filings and governance materials available on Verizon’s investor website; filings also on SEC.gov.

- Forward-looking statements: Safe harbor statement outlining uncertainties and drivers that could cause results to differ, including cybersecurity, infrastructure damage, public health crises, supply chain/geopolitical/climate impacts, labor matters, competition, technology execution (including 5G), strategy execution, economic conditions, regulatory changes, indebtedness, litigation, credit markets/ratings, benefit plan costs, tax and accounting changes.

- Risk factors (Item 1A excerpt):
  - Cyber attacks on Verizon or its ecosystem could cause operational disruption, data loss, reputational harm, legal exposure and financial impacts.
  - Natural disasters, extreme weather, terrorism and climate-related events could damage infrastructure, disrupt services, and increase recovery costs.
  - Public health crises (e.g., COVID-19) could adversely affect operations, demand, collections, workforce availability, supply chain and financial results.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase: The following discussion of "Risk Factors" identifies factors that may adversely affect our business, operations, financial condition or future performance.
structure.summary:
- Notes that changes in tax laws/treaties and accounting rules or their interpretation could impact earnings and forward-looking statements.
- Item 1A. Risk Factors:
  - Operational risks: escalating cybersecurity threats (malware, ransomware, DDoS, social engineering) with potential for service disruption, data loss, costs, litigation, and reputational harm; vulnerability to natural disasters, extreme weather, climate change impacts, and hostile acts; exposure to public health crises such as COVID-19 affecting revenues, costs, supply chains, workforce, and customer demand; reliance on key suppliers and vendors (including single-source components) and related supply chain disruptions or IP litigation; labor relations risks with a significant unionized workforce, potential added costs or work stoppages.
  - Economic and strategic risks: intense competition across telecom, cable, satellite, tech, devices, and apps; need to innovate and meet shifting consumer demand; execution and regulatory risks around 5G deployment and phasing out legacy technologies; adverse macroeconomic conditions (recession, inflation) that may reduce demand and increase delinquencies.
  - Regulatory and legal risks: extensive regulation by the FCC and other authorities domestically and abroad, with licensing and compliance uncertainties; evolving privacy/data protection regimes (e.g., GDPR, CCPA, state laws) with significant penalties; potential shifts in broadband regulation/net neutrality at federal and state levels; “open access” obligations on certain spectrum; climate-related regulation and energy/fuel cost impacts; substantial litigation exposure (shareholder, patent, antitrust, labor, personal injury, advertising/billing practices, and alleged wireless health effects) that could lead to significant defense costs or settlements.
  - Financial risks: high debt levels and related constraints on cash flow, flexibility, and sensitivity to interest rates; potential increases in borrowing costs or limited financing access due to credit market conditions and ratings; rising pension and healthcare costs and funding requirements driven by healthcare inflation, asset returns, and actuarial assumptions.
- Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments: None.
- Item 2. Properties: Gross PP&E of ~$290B at 12/31/2021 (vs. ~$280B in 2020), primarily network equipment (~77%), with the remainder in land/buildings and furniture/other; assets include owned switching centers and widespread U.S. facilities (offices, care centers, retail, garages, cell sites, data centers).
- Item 3. Legal Proceedings: No environmental proceedings likely to result in monetary sanctions of $1 million or more.
- Item 4. Mine Safety Disclosures: None.

structure.title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.heading: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase:
Verizon Communications Inc. (Verizon or the Company) is a holding company that, acting through its subsidiaries, is one of the world’s 
leading providers of communications, technology, information and entertainment products and services to consumers, businesses and 
government entities.
structure.summary:
- Equity and shareholders: Verizon’s common stock trades on NYSE (VZ); 484,764 shareholders of record as of December 31, 2021. A 2020 authorization allows repurchase of up to 100 million shares; no share repurchases in 2020–2021.
- Stock performance: Five-year total return comparison shows Verizon underperformed the S&P 500 and the S&P 500 Telecommunications Services Index through 2021.
- Company overview and strategy: Verizon focuses on network leadership, expanding 4G/5G, the Intelligent Edge Network, fiber investment, and monetizing platforms/solutions for consumers, businesses, and government. Significant, consistent capital investment underpins growth.
- Network and technology: Ongoing 4G densification (small cells, in-building, DAS) and 5G deployment. As of 12/31/21, 5G Ultra Wideband in parts of 87 cities; 5G Home in parts of 65 cities; 5G Nationwide via DSS. C-Band launched Jan 2022, reaching ~100 million POPs by Feb 2022.
- COVID-19: 2021 comparability impacted versus 2020; continued monitoring of variants; no material impact noted thus far in 2021.
- 2021 consolidated financial highlights:
  - Revenues $133.6B (+4.1% YoY); operating income $32.4B; net income $22.6B.
  - Operating cash flow $39.5B; capital expenditures $20.3B (incl. ~$2.1B C-Band-related).
  - Adjusted EBITDA (non-GAAP) $48.4B (vs. $47.1B in 2020).
- Segment structure and performance:
  - Consumer (wireless, Fios, copper; includes FWA): Revenue $95.3B (+7.6%); growth in wireless service and equipment; Fios internet connections up; Fios video down; impact from TracFone acquisition in Q4 2021; churn and ARPA metrics disclosed.
  - Business (wireless and wireline solutions, IoT, FWA): Revenue $31.0B (+0.3%); Small & Medium Business up; declines in Global Enterprise, Public Sector and Wholesale due to secular wireline pressures; equipment revenue up; margins slightly lower.
  - Corporate and other: Lower revenue due to Verizon Media sale in Sept 2021.
- Consolidated operating expenses: Up 1.7% driven by higher wireless equipment costs (mix shift to 5G and higher volumes) and higher rent/content/utilities/regulatory fees; SG&A down (gains on Verizon Media sale, lower provision for credit losses, lower personnel; partially offset by higher advertising).
- Other results:
  - Other income (expense), net improved (pension/postretirement remeasurement gain offset by higher early debt redemption costs).
  - Interest expense down (higher capitalized interest on C-Band; lower average rates despite higher average debt).
  - Effective tax rate 23.1% (slightly lower; Verizon Media sale and 2020 nonrecurring items).
- Special items: Severance costs; pension/postretirement MTM credits in 2021 (charges in 2020); spectrum license losses (smaller in 2021 vs 2020); early debt redemption costs; net gain on dispositions (notably Verizon Media, Complex Media) vs. prior-year loss on HuffPost.
- Outlook and trends (2022+):
  - Growth from migrations to higher-priced plans, content bundles, more devices per account, FWA, and 5G; continued pressure in legacy wireline and linear video.
  - TracFone: near-term retention pressure; longer-term growth targeted via investment and expanded offerings.
  - Ongoing cost efficiency programs (Business Excellence, zero-based budgeting, IT evolution).
- Liquidity and capital resources:
  - Sources sufficient for next 12 months and beyond; cash and equivalents $2.9B at 12/31/21.
  - 2022 capex guidance $16.5–$17.5B plus $5–$6B C-Band-related.
  - Contractual obligations detailed for debt/principal and interest, leases, purchase commitments, and benefit payments.
  - Cash flows: Operating $39.5B (down YoY on working capital and taxes, partly offset by earnings); Investing $(67.2)B (C-Band spectrum, capex; proceeds from Verizon Media sale); Financing $8.3B net inflow (new borrowings incl. ABS; repayments; dividends).
  - Free cash flow (non-GAAP) $19.3B (vs. $23.6B in 2020).
- Capital structure and financing:
  - Total debt $150.9B (vs. $129.1B); effective interest rate 3.6%; significant fixed-rate mix; FX-denominated debt hedged via cross-currency swaps.
  - Asset-backed debt $14.2B secured by device payment plan receivables; new 2021 ABS financing facility ($4.3B borrowed).
  - Revolving credit facility capacity $9.5B (unused); export credit facilities outstanding $4.7B.
  - Dividends: 2.0% quarterly increase in 2021; $10.4B paid in 2021. No share repurchases.
  - Credit ratings unchanged; covenant compliance affirmed.
- Acquisitions and divestitures:
  - TracFone acquisition (Nov 23, 2021): ~$3.5B cash (net), ~57.6M VZ shares (~$3.0B), up to $650M contingent consideration; integration impact noted.
  - Bluegrass Cellular assets acquired (Mar 2021); BlueJeans acquired (May 2020).
  - Verizon Media sold to Apollo affiliate (Sep 1, 2021): ~$4.3B cash, preferred and common partnership units; ~$1.0B pre-tax gain; HuffPost sold (2020/closed 2021); Complex Media investment sold (gain).
  - Spectrum: C-Band Auction 107—~$45.5B licenses paid 2021 plus clearing/incentive obligations (~$7.7B estimated; $1.3B paid 2021; $1.4B paid Jan 2022); prior auctions (Auction 103, Auction 105) detailed.
- Commitments and other matters:
  - Renewable energy purchase agreements totaling up to ~2.6 GW across multiple states.
  - Guarantees, letters of credit (~$674M), leasing arrangements, and asset-backed structures described.
- Critical accounting estimates: Impairment testing for wireless licenses (Greenfield approach) and goodwill (DCF and market methods)—no impairments; pension/postretirement assumptions and sensitivity; income tax uncertainties; PP&E useful lives; CECL for receivables with model sensitivities.
- Competitive environment: Intense competition from national carriers, cable resellers, and technology platforms; high smartphone penetration; 5G expected to drive future growth in both Consumer and Business; pricing and promotions remain key.

structure.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.heading: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.start_phrase: We are exposed to various types of market risk in the normal course of business, including the impact of interest rate changes, foreign currency exchange rate fluctuations, changes in investment, equity and commodity prices and changes in corporate tax rates.
structure.summary:
- Scope of market risk: exposure to interest rate changes, foreign currency fluctuations, investment/equity/commodity price movements, and corporate tax rate changes.
- Risk management strategy: use of derivatives solely for hedging (not trading) to optimize market risk exposure; instruments include cross-currency swaps, forward starting interest rate swaps, interest rate swaps/caps, treasury rate locks, and FX forwards; objective to maintain a prudent fixed/variable debt mix and limit earnings and cash flow volatility without fully eliminating it.
- Counterparty and collateral: derivatives under ISDA/CSA agreements with rating-based collateral thresholds; no offsetting of derivative fair values with collateral balances; collateral at 12/31/21—held $0.1B and posted an insignificant amount (recorded in Other current liabilities and Prepaid expenses and other); at 12/31/20—held $0.2B (Other current liabilities); credit risk from counterparties considered remote due to diversification.
- Interest rate risk profile: as of 12/31/21, ~81% of total debt at fixed rates (including swaps); a 100 bps change in rates on floating-rate debt (including hedges) would change annual interest expense by ~$288M; existing long-term debt rates are not affected by credit rating changes.
- LIBOR transition: certain instruments reference LIBOR; one-week and two-month USD LIBOR ceased after 12/31/21; remaining USD LIBOR to cease after 6/30/23; potential cost impacts not expected to be significant given debt mix and hedging; some new issuances/derivatives use SOFR.
- Fair value sensitivity (long-term debt and related interest rate swap derivatives):
  - 12/31/21: fair value $169,179M; +100 bps $156,078M; -100 bps $184,496M.

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition

nodes.start_phrase: We earn revenue from contracts with customers, primarily through the provision of telecommunications and other services and through the sale of wireless equipment.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Verizon’s business as a global communications, technology, information and entertainment provider operating through two reportable segments: Consumer (wireless, FWA, Fios fiber and copper wireline) and Business (wireless/wireline services, networking, security/managed services, voice, IoT, and FWA) with U.S. focus and select international offerings.

- Revenue recognition: application of ASC 606 for most customer contracts; identification of non-Topic 606 revenues (leasing of towers/equipment, captive reinsurance for device insurance, and interest on agent-originated device payment plans).
- Telecommunications services:
  - Wireless: revenue recognized over time via output methods (usage or passage of time); monthly billing in advance creates contract liabilities; overage recognized when incurred.
  - Wireline: fixed fees billed in advance (contract liabilities) and recognized over the enforceable term; usage-based fees billed in arrears and recognized as incurred.
- Equipment sales: revenue recognized upon delivery/acceptance; two primary offerings—fixed-term plans (device discounted or no upfront charge with a service term) and device payment plans (non-interest-bearing installments with month-to-month service); promotional bill credits included in transaction price and recognized when earned; financing component exists but not significant in direct channel.
- Wireless contract accounting: transaction price allocated between service and equipment using standalone selling prices (retail price for devices; month-to-month service price without term); assessment of legally enforceable rights/obligations (e.g., early termination penalties, cessation of credits) affects service term and transaction price.
- Trade-in/upgrade promotions: accounted for as guarantee obligations that reduce equipment revenue and are outside ASC 606; disclosed guarantee liability of $77 million at December 31, 2021.

nodes.title: Nature of Products and Services

nodes.summary:
- Identifies revenue streams outside ASC 606: leasing (towers/equipment), captive reinsurance for device insurance, and interest on equipment financed under device payment plans when sold through authorized agents.
- Describes telecom service revenue recognition:
  - Wireless: revenue recognized using an output method as allowance units are used or as time elapses; monthly service billed in advance creating contract liabilities; overage charges treated as customer options and recognized when exercised.
  - Wireline: fixed monthly fees billed one month in advance (contract liabilities); revenue recognized over the enforceable term as services are rendered; usage-based charges billed in arrears and recognized as incurred.
- Details equipment revenue recognition:
  - Devices and accessories recognized upon delivery and customer acceptance (control transfer).
  - Two device offerings linked to service: fixed-term plans (device free/discounted for a service commitment up to ~24 months) and device payment plans (non-interest-bearing installments over ~24–30 months with month-to-month service).
  - Promotional billing credits included in the transaction price, allocated based on relative standalone selling prices, recognized when earned.
- Addresses financing components in device arrangements:
  - Financing exists because payment occurs over time while control transfers at inception.
  - Regular assessment of significance using commercial objectives, term, market rates, and customer credit risk.
  - Conclusion: financing component in direct-channel fixed-term and device payment plans is not significant and not accounted for separately; separate note references interest on indirect-channel financed equipment.
- Explains allocation of transaction price in wireless contracts:
  - Allocated between service and equipment based on estimated standalone selling prices.
  - Standalone equipment price is retail (excluding subsidies/conditional discounts); standalone service price is the month-to-month, no-commitment rate or service-only rate.
  - Considers legally enforceable rights/obligations (e.g., early termination penalties, cessation of credits) in determining service term and transaction price.
- Accounts for device upgrade trade-in promotions:
  - Trade-in right treated as a guarantee; fair value recorded as a guarantee liability that reduces device revenue.
  - Guarantee is outside ASC 606; remaining transaction price allocated to in-scope performance obligations.
  - Reported guarantee liability of $77 million at December 31, 2021 (insignificant in 2020).

nodes.title: Telecommunications Service

- Outlines allocation of total wireless contract consideration between service and equipment using estimated standalone selling prices: devices at retail price excluding subsidies; service at month-to-month price without fixed term or without bundled device; considers legally enforceable terms (e.g., early termination penalties, cessation of credits) that affect transaction price and service term.

nodes.title: Equipment

- Describes service revenue recognition:

nodes.title: Wireless Contracts

- Explains equipment revenue: recognized upon delivery/acceptance; two primary offerings—fixed-term plans (often subsidized device tied to service term) and device payment plans (non‑interest‑bearing installments over 24–30 months with month‑to‑month service); promotions via billing credits included in transaction price and allocated by relative standalone selling prices (SSP).

- Principal vs. agent assessments for offers including third parties: based on control, fulfillment responsibility, risk of loss, and pricing discretion.
- Other revenues: advertising (display and search) recognized as ads are delivered; subscription advertising recognized over time; generally principal on advertising platforms (gross reporting); Verizon Media sale completed 9/1/2021. Telematics revenues primarily from subscriptions recognized over time. Taxes collected from customers reported on a net basis.

nodes.title: Wireline Contracts
nodes.heading: Wireline Contracts
nodes.start_phrase: Total consideration for wireline services that are bundled in a single contract is allocated to each performance obligation based on our standalone selling price for each service.
nodes.summary:
- Revenue recognition for wireless fixed-term plans: subsidized device sales create contract assets when recognized equipment revenue exceeds amounts billed. Device payment plan billing credits are treated as consideration payable, included in transaction price, and recorded as contract liabilities.
- Variable consideration: rights of return, credits, and incentives (including for resellers and Business customers) are estimated at contract inception, included in transaction price, and updated each reporting period; revenue recognized net of expected returns.

nodes.title: Intangible Assets Not Subject to Amortization
nodes.heading: Intangible Assets Not Subject to Amortization
nodes.start_phrase: A significant portion of our intangible assets are wireless licenses that provide our wireless operations with the exclusive right to utilize designated radio frequency spectrum to provide wireless communication services.
nodes.summary:
- Wireless licenses are treated as indefinite-lived intangible assets due to routine, low-cost FCC renewals and no limiting legal, regulatory, competitive, or economic factors; useful life assessment is re-evaluated annually, and licenses are aggregated into a single unit of accounting given their integrated nationwide use.
- Impairment testing for wireless licenses is performed annually or upon indicators; the company may use a qualitative screen or proceed directly to a quantitative test, which it performs at least every three years by policy.
- Qualitative assessment considers enterprise value, macroeconomic conditions (including interest/discount rates), industry trends, M&A activity, and business performance.
- Quantitative assessment estimates fair value using the Greenfield (income-based DCF) approach to value a hypothetical start-up holding only the licenses; impairments are recognized if aggregated fair value is below carrying amount.
- Interest incurred during qualifying activities to ready wireless licenses for use is capitalized; capitalization ends when the license is ready for intended use or development ceases.
- FCC auction deposits for licenses are recorded as Deposits for wireless licenses on the balance sheet and as investing cash flows until licenses are received.
- Intangible assets with finite lives (e.g., customer lists, internal-use software) are amortized over estimated useful lives; they and other long-lived assets are tested for impairment upon indicators using an undiscounted cash flow recoverability test, followed by fair value measurement if not recoverable; useful lives are reassessed annually.
- Lease accounting: the company leases network equipment (towers, DAS, small cells), real estate, dark fiber, equipment, and other assets; identifies leases at inception and measures right-of-use assets and lease liabilities at commencement for both operating and finance leases.
- Lease liabilities are measured at the present value of lease payments using an incremental borrowing rate determined via a portfolio approach, starting with the unsecured rate and risk-adjusting to approximate a collateralized rate; rates are updated quarterly.
- Cross-reference to Note 4 for details on carrying amounts, components, and useful lives of goodwill, wireless licenses, and other intangible assets.

nodes.heading: Leases

- Capitalization related to licenses: Interest incurred during qualifying activities to ready licenses for use is capitalized; FCC auction deposits are recorded as Deposits for wireless licenses on the balance sheet and as investing cash outflows until licenses are received.
- Intangible assets subject to amortization and long-lived assets: Customer lists and internal-use software are amortized over estimated useful lives; assets are tested for recoverability upon impairment indicators using undiscounted cash flows, with fair value measured and impairments recorded if not recoverable; useful lives are reassessed annually.
- Leases (ASC 842): As lessee, the company recognizes right-of-use assets and lease liabilities for operating and finance leases, measured using an incremental borrowing rate derived via a portfolio approach and updated quarterly; non-lease components are combined with lease components for most asset classes; rent for operating leases is straight-lined to Cost of services or SG&A, variable lease payments are expensed as incurred, short-term leases (12 months or less) are off-balance sheet; finance lease amortization is in Depreciation and amortization and interest in Interest expense; as lessor, certain arrangements combine lease and non-lease components under Topic 606 when services predominate.
- Fair value measurements: Applies exit price notion with a three-level hierarchy (Levels 1–3); instruments are classified based on the lowest significant input; significant judgment is required in valuation and categorization.
- Income taxes: Effective tax rate depends on pre-tax income, laws, rates, and planning; deferred taxes recorded for temporary differences with valuation allowances as needed; uncertain tax positions follow a two-step recognition (more-likely-than-not) and measurement process, affecting taxes payable/receivable and deferred tax accounts; significant judgment is involved.
- Stock-based compensation: Measured and recognized at estimated fair value for awards to employees and directors.
- Foreign currency: For most foreign operations, the functional currency is local; income statements are translated at average rates and balance sheet amounts at end-of-period rates.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements
nodes.heading: Fair Value Measurements
nodes.start_phrase: Fair value of financial and non-financial assets and liabilities is defined as an exit price, representing the amount that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants.
nodes.summary:
- Lease accounting policies under ASC 842:
  - As lessee, the company combines lease and non-lease components (e.g., CAM) into a single lease component for most asset classes.
  - As lessor, customer premise equipment arrangements combine lease and non-lease components under Topic 606 when service revenue is predominant.
  - Operating lease rent is recognized on a straight-line basis and recorded in Cost of services or SG&A; variable lease payments (taxes, CAM, utilities) are expensed as incurred.
  - Short-term operating leases (12 months or less) are not recognized on the balance sheet; expense is straight-lined.
  - Finance leases: ROU asset amortized straight-line over the shorter of lease term or useful life in Depreciation and amortization; interest expense recognized via effective interest method in Interest expense.
  - Reference to Note 6 for detailed lease disclosures.

- Fair value measurements:
  - Fair value defined as exit price; use of a three-level input hierarchy (Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs, Level 3 unobservable inputs).
  - Classification based on the lowest significant input level; valuation and hierarchy placement require judgment.

- Income taxes:
  - Effective tax rate driven by pre-tax income, statutory rates, laws/regulations, and tax planning across jurisdictions.
  - Deferred taxes recorded for temporary differences and remeasured using enacted rates; valuation allowances recorded when realization is not more likely than not.
  - Uncertain tax positions follow a two-step process: recognition (more-likely-than-not) and measurement (largest amount >50% likely upon settlement), affecting taxes payable/refundable and deferred taxes.
  - Significant management judgment involved.

- Stock-based compensation:
  - Compensation expense for employee and director awards measured and recognized based on estimated fair value (see Note 10).

- Foreign currency:
  - Functional currency generally local; translation to U.S. dollars uses average rates for income statement items and end-of-period rates for balance sheet items.

nodes.title: Income Taxes
nodes.heading: Income Taxes
nodes.start_phrase: Our effective tax rate is based on pre-tax income, statutory tax rates, tax laws and regulations and tax planning strategies available to us in the various jurisdictions in which we operate.
nodes.summary:
- Lease accounting policies:
  - As lessee, the company combines lease and non-lease components (e.g., common area maintenance) into a single lease component for most asset classes.
  - As lessor (e.g., customer premise equipment), lease and non-lease components (e.g., service revenue) are combined and accounted for under Topic 606 when service revenue predominates.
  - Operating lease rent expense is recognized on a straight-line basis and recorded in Cost of services or SG&A depending on use; variable lease payments (e.g., taxes, CAM, utilities) are expensed as incurred.
  - Short-term operating leases (12 months or less) are not recorded on the balance sheet; expense is straight-lined over the term.
  - Finance leases: right-of-use asset amortized on a straight-line basis over the shorter of lease term or asset life (in Depreciation and amortization); interest recognized using the effective interest method (in Interest expense).
  - Reference to Note 6 for ASC 842 disclosures.

- Fair value measurements:
  - Fair value defined as exit price in an orderly transaction.
  - Three-level hierarchy: Level 1 (quoted prices in active markets), Level 2 (observable inputs other than quoted prices), Level 3 (unobservable inputs).
  - Classification is based on the lowest significant input; judgment affects valuation and hierarchy placement.

- Income taxes:
  - Effective tax rate depends on pre-tax income, statutory rates, laws/regulations, and tax planning across jurisdictions.
  - Deferred taxes recognized for temporary differences and remeasured annually at enacted rates; valuation allowances recorded when realization is not more likely than not.
  - Uncertain tax positions use a two-step approach: recognition (more-likely-than-not) and measurement (largest benefit with >50% likelihood), with impacts to taxes payable/refundable and deferred taxes.
  - Significant management judgment is required.

- Stock-based compensation:
  - Compensation expense for employee and director awards is measured and recognized based on estimated fair value (see Note 10).

- Foreign currency:
  - Functional currency of foreign operations is generally the local currency.
  - Translation to U.S. dollars uses average exchange rates for income statement amounts and end-of-period exchange rates for balance sheet amounts.

nodes.title: Stock-Based Compensation

  - Finance lease ROU assets are amortized straight-line over the shorter of lease term or asset life; related interest is recognized using the effective interest method. Reference to ASC 842 disclosures (Note 6).

- Fair value measurements:
  - Fair value defined as exit price; use of a three-level input hierarchy (Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs, Level 3 unobservable inputs).

- Income taxes:
  - Effective tax rate driven by pre-tax income, statutory rates, laws/regulations, and tax planning across jurisdictions.

nodes.title: Foreign Currency Translation and Transactions
nodes.heading: Foreign Currency Translation and Transactions
nodes.start_phrase: The functional currency of our foreign operations is generally the local currency.
nodes.summary:
- Lease accounting: As lessee, the company combines lease and non-lease components (e.g., CAM) into a single lease component for most asset classes. As lessor for customer premise equipment, lease and non-lease components (e.g., service revenue) are combined and recognized under Topic 606 since services predominate.
- Operating leases: Rent expense is recognized on a straight-line basis and recorded in Cost of services or SG&A based on usage. Variable lease payments (taxes, CAM, utilities) are expensed as incurred. Short-term leases (12 months or less) are not capitalized and are expensed straight-line.
- Finance leases: Right-of-use assets are amortized straight-line over the shorter of lease term or useful life (in Depreciation and amortization); interest is recognized using the effective interest method (in Interest expense). Reference to Topic 842 disclosures (Note 6).
- Fair value measurements: Defines fair value as exit price and applies a three-level hierarchy (Level 1–3). Assets/liabilities are classified based on the lowest significant input, with judgment impacting valuation and categorization.
- Income taxes: Effective rate driven by pre-tax income, statutes, and planning. Deferred taxes recorded for temporary differences and remeasured at enacted rates; valuation allowances recorded as needed. Uncertain tax positions follow a two-step ASC 740 model (more-likely-than-not recognition and measurement of the largest benefit >50% likely), with resulting impacts on payables, refunds, and deferreds; significant judgment required.
- Stock-based compensation: Expense measured and recognized based on estimated fair values of awards (Note 10).
- Foreign currency: Functional currency generally local; income statement translated at average rates, balance sheet at period-end; translation adjustments recorded in AOCI; transaction gains/losses in Other income (expense), net.
- Employee benefit plans: Pension and postretirement costs accrued for service and interest; prior service cost amortized over average remaining service period; expected return based on actual fair value of assets; actuarial gains/losses recognized in Other income (expense), net when incurred and measured annually or upon remeasurement. Management employees no longer accrue pension benefits or retiree medical subsidy service. Funded status recognized on the balance sheet; certain items recorded in AOCI net of tax.
- Derivatives: Used to manage FX and interest rate risk (e.g., cross-currency swaps, interest rate swaps, caps, forwards, treasury locks); not for trading. All derivatives measured at fair value (primarily Level 2) and recognized on the balance sheet. Accounting by hedge type: economic hedges in current earnings; fair value hedges—both derivative and hedged item changes in earnings; cash flow hedges—OCI then reclassified to earnings; net investment hedges—OCI as CTA. Cash flows classified consistently with hedged items (Note 9).
- Variable interest entities: Defines VIEs and consolidates when the company is the primary beneficiary—i.e., it has the power to direct activities most affecting performance and the obligation to absorb losses or right to receive significant benefits.

nodes.title: Employee Benefit Plans
nodes.heading: Employee Benefit Plans
nodes.start_phrase: Pension and postretirement health care and life insurance benefits earned during the year, as well as interest on projected benefit obligations, are accrued.
nodes.summary:
- Foreign currency: Translation adjustments for assets and liabilities are recorded in Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss within equity; transaction-related exchange gains/losses are recognized in Other income (expense), net.
- Employee benefit plans: Pension and postretirement costs (service and interest) are accrued; prior service costs/credits are generally amortized over employees’ average remaining service period; expected return on assets is based on an assumption applied to actual fair value; actuarial gains/losses are recognized immediately in Other income (expense), net, measured annually at December 31 or upon remeasurement; funded status is recognized on the balance sheet; related prior service amounts flow through AOCI net of tax; Verizon management employees no longer accrue pension benefits or retiree medical subsidy.
- Derivative instruments: Used to manage foreign currency and interest rate risk (e.g., cross-currency swaps, interest rate swaps, forward-starting swaps, treasury locks, caps, FX forwards); not for trading; all derivatives measured at fair value and recorded as assets or liabilities; primarily Level 2 valuations; accounting by hedge type—economic hedges in current earnings, fair value hedges with offsetting changes in earnings, cash flow hedges in OCI then reclassified to earnings, net investment hedges in OCI as part of cumulative translation adjustment; derivative cash flows classified consistently with hedged items.
- Variable Interest Entities (VIEs): Defines VIEs and consolidates them when Verizon is the primary beneficiary—i.e., has power over activities that most affect performance and has exposure to potentially significant benefits or losses.

nodes.title: Derivative Instruments
nodes.heading: Derivative Instruments
nodes.start_phrase: We enter into derivative transactions primarily to manage our exposure to fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates and interest rates.
nodes.summary:
- Foreign currency translation: Translation adjustments from consolidating foreign operations are recorded in Accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOCI), while transaction-related exchange gains and losses are recognized in Other income (expense), net.
- Employee benefit plans: Pension and postretirement benefits are accrued for service and interest costs; prior service costs/credits are amortized over average remaining service; expected return is based on actual fair value of plan assets; actuarial gains/losses are recognized immediately in Other income (expense), net and measured annually at December 31 or upon remeasurement. Funded status is recognized on the balance sheet, with certain items recorded in AOCI net of tax. Verizon management employees no longer accrue pension benefits or retiree medical subsidy.
- Derivative instruments and hedging: The company uses derivatives (e.g., cross-currency swaps, interest rate swaps/caps, treasury locks, FX forwards) for risk management, not trading. All derivatives are measured at fair value (primarily Level 2). Accounting varies by hedge type: economic hedges in current earnings; fair value hedges recognize changes for both derivative and hedged item in earnings; cash flow hedges in OCI and reclassified to earnings with the hedged item; net investment hedges in OCI as part of cumulative translation adjustment. Cash flows are classified consistently with hedged items.
- Variable interest entities (VIEs): Defines VIEs and consolidates them when the company is the primary beneficiary—i.e., has the power to direct significant activities and the obligation to absorb losses or the right to receive potentially significant benefits.

nodes.title: Variable Interest Entities
nodes.heading: Variable Interest Entities
nodes.start_phrase: VIEs are entities that lack sufficient equity to permit the entity to finance its activities without additional subordinated financial support from other parties, have equity investors that do not have the ability to make significant decisions relating to the entity’s operations through voting rights, do not have the obligation to absorb the expected losses, or do not have the right to receive the residual returns of the entity.
nodes.summary:
- Foreign currency: Translation adjustments for assets and liabilities are recorded in Accumulated other comprehensive loss (equity); transaction-related exchange gains/losses are recorded in Other income (expense), net.
- Employee benefit plans: Pension and postretirement service cost and interest are accrued; prior service costs/credits amortized over average remaining service life; expected return based on the assumption applied to actual fair value of plan assets; actuarial gains/losses recognized in Other income (expense), net in the period measured (annually at December 31 or upon remeasurement). Management employees no longer earn pension benefits or service toward the retiree medical subsidy. Funded status recognized as an asset or liability on the balance sheet; new prior service costs/credits recorded in Accumulated other comprehensive income, net of tax.
- Derivative instruments: Used to manage foreign currency and interest rate risk (e.g., cross-currency swaps, interest rate swaps, forward-starting swaps, treasury locks, caps, FX forwards); not for trading. All derivatives measured at fair value and recorded as assets or liabilities; valued primarily with Level 2 inputs. Accounting: economic hedges recognized in current earnings; fair value hedges—derivative and hedged item fair value changes in earnings; cash flow hedges—changes in OCI and reclassified to earnings with the hedged item; net investment hedges—changes in OCI as part of the cumulative translation adjustment. Cash flows classified consistent with the hedged items.
- Variable interest entities: Defines VIE characteristics and consolidates VIEs when the company is the primary beneficiary—i.e., has power over key activities and exposure to potentially significant benefits or losses.

nodes.title: Recently Adopted Accounting Standards

nodes.title: Remaining Performance Obligations
nodes.heading: Remaining Performance Obligations
nodes.start_phrase: When allocating the total contract transaction price to identified performance obligations, a portion of the total transaction price may relate to service performance obligations which were not satisfied or are partially satisfied as of the end of the reporting period.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on ASC 606 Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO) and Accounts Receivable/Contract Balances.
- Practical expedient applied to exclude RPO for contracts with original duration of one year or less; many services are month-to-month.
- Month-to-month prevalence:
  - At Dec 31, 2021: ~93% of wireless postpaid; ~86% of wireline Consumer and Small/Medium Business (SMB).
  - At Dec 31, 2020: ~90% of wireless postpaid; ~75% of wireline Consumer and SMB.
- Wireless contracts:
  - Often month-to-month and cancellable (e.g., under device payment plans) or fixed-term up to ~30 months.
  - Usage-based charges and optional add-on services recognized when incurred; excluded from initial transaction price.
  - Unsatisfied service obligations largely tied to non–month-to-month contracts.
- Wholesale/reseller arrangements (Consumer group):
  - Multi-year terms, often >2 years, sometimes with periodic minimum revenue commitments recognized in future periods.
- Wireline contracts:
  - Consumer: generally month-to-month; some up to two years or under 12 months.
  - Business: many terms ≤12 months; others extend further with fixed monthly and usage fees, with annual or total-term commitments.
- Certain Business wireline and telematics contracts have contractual minimum fees over terms extending up to August 2031; $2.4 billion aggregate minimums; excluded from RPO time bands due to uncertain revenue timing.
- RPO at Dec 31, 2021 expected to be recognized:
  - 2022: $17.0 billion
  - 2023: $8.3 billion
  - Thereafter: $2.3 billion
  - Subject to change for terminations and contract modifications.
- Accounts Receivable vs. Contract Balances:
  - Receivables represent unconditional rights to consideration; contract balances arise from performance before billing or customer prepayments before transfer.
- Receivables data (in millions):
  - Receivables: $10,758 (12/31/21); $12,029 (12/31/20); $12,078 (1/1/20).
  - Device payment plan agreement receivables: $12,888 (12/31/21); $10,358 (12/31/20); $11,741 (1/1/20).
- Receivables exclude amounts from leasing (towers/equipment), captive reinsurance for device insurance, and interest on equipment financed under device plans when sold by authorized agents.
- Device payment plan receivables include amounts related to equipment sold on device plans through authorized agents (cross-referenced to Note 8).

nodes.title: Accounts Receivable and Contract Balances
nodes.heading: Accounts Receivable and Contract Balances
nodes.start_phrase: The timing of revenue recognition may differ from the time of billing to our customers.
nodes.summary:
- Describes Verizon’s application of ASC 606 to remaining performance obligations (RPOs), including use of the practical expedient to exclude unsatisfied obligations for contracts with original terms of one year or less.
- Notes the prevalence of month-to-month contracts: at December 31, 2021, ~93% of wireless postpaid and 86% of wireline Consumer/SMB were month-to-month (vs. ~90% and 75% at December 31, 2020).
- Explains that fees for optional/add-on services are recognized when exercised (typically month-to-month) and that usage-based charges and cancellable options are excluded from the transaction price.
- Outlines wireless contract types (month-to-month/device payment plans and fixed-term plans up to 30 months) and that non–month-to-month contracts drive most unsatisfied service performance obligations at period-end.
- Discusses Consumer wholesale reseller arrangements with multi-year terms (often >2 years) that may include periodic minimum revenue commitments recognized in future periods.
- Describes wireline contracts: Consumer generally month-to-month (some up to two years or <12 months); Business contracts often ≤12 months but can include fixed monthly and usage fees with annual or total-term commitments.
- Highlights certain Business wireline and telematics contracts with contractual minimum fees totaling $2.4 billion through August 2031; timing of revenue recognition is unpredictable, so they are excluded from RPO time bands.
- Provides RPO time-band amounts at December 31, 2021: $17.0 billion expected in 2022, $8.3 billion in 2023, and $2.3 billion thereafter; subject to change with contract modifications or terminations.
- Explains differences between revenue recognition and billing; defines receivables (unconditional rights) and contract balances (assets/liabilities from timing differences in performance vs. consideration).
- Presents receivables data: receivables of $10,758 million (2021), $12,029 million (2020); device payment plan receivables of $12,888 million (2021), $10,358 million (2020); excludes leasing, captive reinsurance, and certain agent-financed interest.
- Details contract assets: $934 million (2021) vs. $937 million (2020); arise mainly from equipment revenue recognized up front under fixed-term plans; reclassified to accounts receivable as services are billed; credit loss allowance recognized at inception; 2020 decrease of $213 million included $75 million impairment.
- Details contract liabilities: $7,229 million (2021) vs. $5,598 million (2020); primarily advance billing of service; 2021 increase driven by promotions recognized over time, upfront fees, higher advance billings, and the TracFone acquisition, partially offset by satisfaction of obligations and the Verizon Media sale; revenue recognized from beginning contract liabilities was $4.3 billion in both 2021 and 2020.
- Shows balance sheet placement: contract assets in Prepaid expenses and other ($739 million) and Other assets ($195 million); contract liabilities in Other current liabilities ($6,053 million) and Other liabilities ($1,176 million) at December 31, 2021.
- Explains capitalization of incremental costs to obtain contracts (commissions) under ASC 606 and amortization: wireless costs over estimated device upgrade cycles for Consumer and Business; wireline Consumer over estimated customer relationship period; Business wireline incremental costs are insignificant; costs recorded in SG&A.

nodes.title: Contract Costs
nodes.heading: Contract Costs
nodes.start_phrase: As discussed in Note 1, Topic 606 requires the recognition of an asset for incremental costs to obtain a customer contract, which are then amortized to expense over the respective periods of expected benefit.
nodes.summary:
- Presents contract balances with amounts: contract assets of $934m (2021), $937m (2020), $1,150m (1/1/2020); contract liabilities of $7,229m (2021), $5,598m (2020), $5,307m (1/1/2020).
- Explains contract assets under ASC 606: created mainly by fixed-term wireless plans when equipment revenue recognized exceeds customer consideration at delivery; reclassified to accounts receivable as services are billed; allowance for credit losses recognized at inception and reassessed quarterly; presented in Prepaid expenses and other and Other assets.
- Notes changes in contract assets: relatively flat in 2021; decreased $213m in 2020 due to billings and $75m impairments, partly offset by new wireless contracts.
- Describes contract liabilities: arise from advance billings (primarily one month in advance for service); recognized as revenue as services are provided; presented in Other current liabilities and Other liabilities.
- Notes changes in contract liabilities: up $1.6b in 2021 (sales promotions recognized over time, upfront fees, advanced billings, Tracfone acquisition; partially offset by satisfied performance obligations and Verizon Media sale); up $291m in 2020 (similar drivers minus acquisitions/divestitures). Revenue recognized from opening contract liabilities was $4.3b for both 2021 and 2020.
- Provides balance sheet detail at 12/31/21 vs 12/31/20: contract assets split between Prepaid expenses and other ($739m/$733m) and Other assets ($195m/$204m); contract liabilities split between Other current liabilities ($6,053m/$4,843m) and Other liabilities ($1,176m/$755m).
- Details contract costs: capitalize incremental costs to obtain contracts (commissions) and certain fulfillment costs (e.g., wireline circuit installations) when recoverable; amortize on a portfolio basis over 2–6 years. Wireless commission costs amortized over estimated device upgrade cycles; consumer wireline over relationship period; business wireline incremental costs insignificant. Costs to obtain recorded in SG&A; fulfillment costs expensed in Cost of services. Deferred contract costs totaled $4,691m at 12/31/21 ($2,432m current; $2,259m noncurrent) vs $4,542m at 12/31/20. Amortization expense was $3.0b (2021) and $3.1b (2020). No impairments in 2021 or 2020.
- Summarizes spectrum license transactions:
